comparison: Both evaluate the mechanistic hypothesis about spatial distribution of contrast and visual field effects (C46-C53). OpenEval finds the hypothesis well-supported by citations and logical inference, though notes C52-C53 are speculative. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this mechanism by not challenging it and focusing on methodological clarifications instead.

Both address the perception-action link (C85-C88). OpenEval finds strong support from consistent correspondence between perceptual and behavioral experiments. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, questioning whether haptic feedback from the steering wheel could confound the behavioral results, suggesting effects may not be purely perceptual.

Both evaluate the main theoretical contribution about spatial distribution determining perceived speed (C74-C84). OpenEval finds strong support from all four experiments. Peer reviewers explicitly state the manuscript makes 'an important and interesting contribution meriting publication,' accepting the core conclusion despite requesting methodological clarifications.

Both address characterization of prior research (C1, C2, C8-C11). OpenEval finds accurate characterization with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these background claims by not questioning them, focusing instead on novel findings about distance-dependent contrast.

Both evaluate methodological justification for simplified stimuli (C89-C97). OpenEval finds the design choice defensible for isolating perceptual mechanisms, though notes some claims are speculative. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about ecological validity, noting 'impoverished detail compared to real life driving' and requesting discussion of how stimulus choice affects self-motion estimation.

Both address adequacy of visual flow in simplified environment (C98-C104). OpenEval finds empirical evidence of accurate baseline performance validates the approach. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about ecological validity and note inconsistencies between figures showing different scene details, raising questions about actual stimuli used.

Both evaluate Experiment 3 findings with anti-fog manipulation (C54-C63). OpenEval finds well-designed critical test with significant results supporting the hypothesis. Peer reviewers don't explicitly critique this experiment but raise general statistical clarity concerns and question potential contrast adaptation effects and extended session duration (1.5 hrs).

Both evaluate Experiment 4 behavioral validation (C64-C70). OpenEval finds appropriate statistics and interesting additional finding about increased variability in anti-fog condition. Peer reviewers express same general concerns as for Experiment 3, particularly questioning the extended trial duration in Experiment 4.

Both evaluate Experiment 1 primary findings (C23-C29). OpenEval finds appropriate statistical support for main effects, interactions, and post-hoc comparisons. Peer reviewers find contribution important but express uncertainty due to unclear statistical presentation, noting 'error bars are unspecified' and ANOVA details are 'missing,' making full evaluation difficult.

Both evaluate Experiment 2 behavioral findings (C33-C41). OpenEval finds appropriate statistical support with consistent patterns across conditions. Peer reviewers accept the contribution as important but raise same statistical presentation concerns, making it difficult to fully evaluate claim strength.

Both evaluate synthesis of Experiments 1-2 showing spatial distribution matters (C42-C45). OpenEval finds strong support from opposite effects with matched global contrast. Peer reviewers accept importance but express uncertainty due to statistical presentation issues affecting evaluation of these synthesized claims.

Both address main contributions including replication and novel fog findings (C3-C5, C73, C131-C135). OpenEval finds claims well-supported by all experiments with justified novelty. Peer reviewers find contribution 'important and interesting' but express uncertainty due to statistical presentation concerns that affect evaluation of these summary claims.

OpenEval evaluates physical properties of fog (C14-C17, C77) as well-established atmospheric physics facts. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims about fog properties.

OpenEval evaluates identification of literature gap regarding distance-dependent contrast (C12-C13, C18-C21) as logically sound and well-justified. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific gap identification claims.
